It would have been a wonderful thing that someone who takes old pictures back in those days.
There aren't any. So you see, what we're trying to do is to get some paintings of that thing.

We're just talking to everyone to try to find out how to look. We need information from the musicians who are there, so it's accurate. You see? Like we played, we used to play those excursions every Sunday. They go about 90 miles, 100, I don't know all the things. You mean on the train? We played on the train all the way to this stop where we were going. Sometimes they go home to Louisiana, Tibidale, Louisiana, and they always have two, three picnics there, and all the bands would meet us after training. That's what you want? Yeah, yeah. Let's start with one. This is Pops Foster. Well you can put that in after. All the bands I got. All the bands, they'd have three or four different bands. One of the best bands gets the most crowd at the pavilion where they was playing. There was no pavilion. It was just a lot, you know, and dancing on the ground. I mean on the ground.
Like on grass, you mean? No.

They have floors or something? No, no floors. They were scraped what they call... Claude. Claude. Claude is in Creole, it's Claude, but it's a hard lump of date, see, but in Creole that's Claude. I see. I know. And they would get like a rake and scrape all that off. They'd get it smooth. What did they dance there? Dance on that? Just on the ground. On the ground, yeah. And all the hard pebbles, you know, that's what we call Claude's back in those days.
I see. You mean this is where out in the country?

It's where out in the country. I don't know, there's big trees, picnics. You don't have to worry about carrying no food, because everybody had a basket. And back in those days, you used to drink. Had the very best wine, the Claret wines, Italian Claret wine. You had the best wine and stuff.
You supposed to recall the Claret wine, Fox? Is that the name?

Oh, yeah. Well, everybody would bring their baskets. Uh-huh. Would hide it, by the bandstand. Well, who used to watch for the best basket? We'd steal the best wine out of that basket. About when would you say this was, what you said? Well, this was around 1910. Around 1910. Yeah. And we'd catch the train at 7 o'clock in the morning. And the train, see, the train, back at that time, there wasn't no bridge in New Orleans. See, the train would leave from down the Esplanade Street in the river. See, the train would go over, the coaches would go over on a flat car, see. Go over, it's not, it's between Algea's, there's a little town, I forget the name of it, let me see, Algea's. Between Algea's. The train would pick up that Southern Pacific train. Where the steam engine would be waiting on the other side for that. Oh. The boat comes in with the train. They pull the coaches off, then we'd go up an hour, next stop would be in Gretton, Louisiana, and we'd pick up people. Sometimes I used to sleep too late. And I had to catch the train in Gretton, Louisiana. I couldn't catch the train downtown. And we'd go to like Homer, Thibodeau, where the train would branch off and stay there until 6 o'clock in the evening and then come on back, see, where the train would go. And it was a dollar for that trip on the train, you know. It was plenty of fun.
Both ways? You mean return trips? There's a dollar, there's a dollar for the dollar, the car charged a dollar on the excursion. Uh-huh. See? For the whole thing?
For the whole thing.
And they stopped on the way and people would join?
They don't care how close it was, it still was a dollar. See?
I see. It was one price.

And then I, now they're going to this picnic ground where it was, it didn't cost you over a quarter. And if they were selling tickets, if you had a ticket, you'd pay 15 cents with that ticket. Oh, yeah. And that was plenty of money to spend back in those days. It was a lot of fun. What kind of band did you have there? Well you had a seven piece band, that was a big band. You had your violin, guitar, drums, bass, clarinet, trombone, and trumpet. No piano. You didn't see no piano. If piano players back in those days would want to learn anything, want to play in these bands, they had to learn how to play something, drums or something. Yeah. In those days were you bowing or were you? I was born in picking. Both. Yeah. You see, they claimed that I was the first one started that, but I was the first one made it famous, but I was the first one started. Who do you think it was? Well I don't know as far back as I can remember. People were picking. Picking, see. But they wasn't playing as fast forward like I played, see, I think I picked that up out of nowhere. I can't tell you when. Because I was born in the United States. I think I used to do that when I was in the Rayleigh Light District. I'm
not sure. When you started to pick, were you playing like a four beats to a- Yeah. It was a four beats to a bar. Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. See, there

used to be two, boom, boom, see. It's like when I come to New York, they had a two beats to a bar. So when I started picking the four, they'll come up, the publishers never got wide, and come up there and started writing four beats to a bar. And then fast numbers the two players couldn't play that, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, see. So that's why everybody tried to learn a string bass and I was shaming the camera string bass around. Now I always wanted to play tuba, you know, I was in Los Angeles in 22. And I come out there, was it 22? Were you playing with Ori then? I was in Ori, yeah, I was with Ori. Yeah, I think it was in 22. I went out there to play tuba and I broke the middle vowel. No, it was 27. Broke the middle vowel on my tuba. And this boy asked him could I pick his name was Bagnet. I said, Mr. Bagnet, I said I broke the middle vowel. Like on Friday I couldn't get it fixed. He said, where are the string bass down? So I heard string bass out of the crowd around, so he told me, so you can't get this in. I said, what string bass is. I like this, but I do the tuba. And that's the way it went through the tuba. Then I started demonstrating string bass at the Platte Music Store in Los Angeles. Is that so? Yeah. The Platte Music Store, Hill Street. I know where it is, sure. And Carnes and Buescher. I think the Platte Music Store was on, what's it, Maine I think, right off of 12th Street. I think so, somewhere around there. It's been a long time listening up. It's still there. But then I started playing
the string bass. Now, Pops, let's get a little background on you. Where were you born?

McCall, Louisiana, or Assumption Parish. I said Louisiana, that's about 68 miles from New Orleans, going towards Baton Rouge. I was about to say that was west. Yes. What year? 1892. 19th day of May. See, now this is, see 19, the next one ought to be 65.
Uh-huh. Well, you certainly look in marvelous shape. You're in great shape. I hope I look
as good as you do when I'm 65. Well, let's make it to me. Let me see how you look when you get 35. I don't care if it's wounded or let me see. Well, it was.
How did you first get interested in music, Pops? You see, my brother, I had an uncle, my father,

my uncle used to play a little ham fat violin, they called it, see, but all my mother's people played music. Oh yeah? See, all of them. What was the ham fat violin? Well you know, just play it around like, they used to call it the brulee. You played the dancing for the Cajuns. Now Cajuns, there's a verse of them you hear that word called, Cajuns. Now Cajuns, they're funny people. They ain't white, and they ain't colored. They're colored, but they don't want to be colored, and they don't want to be white. So they call themselves Cajuns, Cajuns. That's what you call half and half. You see, they can get that half and a half mil. That's funny back in those days, man. And he was playing for them? Well I played for them, my uncle played for them. See? Well then, you played a little part of Zen, but you had a three piece band like guitar, violin, and bass. Or mandolin, guitar, and bass. Now when my sister started playing, my sister played mandolin. Well my brother played guitar and my sister played mandolin. Well we played in big hard jars, my brother played violin, and regettas are guitar players. Sometime we used to get a violin, a violin, a violin player, and play those big picnics. That's why my schooling was very weak. All the kind of music. When we were young babies back then. Because they'd play music. And everything the school, any school kid, when he was invited, to play in that concert. When exams come up, you don't have to go through exams. See, and I thought it was great. But you relate your feelings, you know what I mean? See that's why I didn't want none of them. The kids that was connected with me, I didn't have none of them. All my kids died, see, by my first wife. And my wife's got a cousin, he's got a lot of kids, and they all crazy about me. Well one of the oldest ones wanted to play string bass, well I couldn't see it, but he still wanted to play it. Well he's playing it in school, in New York, see. Oh yeah. See what goes here. And I got an exam and they had a rehearsal, he said, I've got to miss the exam today, and I heard it. See. I told his dad, he said, oh no, don't let him miss that exam. I said, let him go through his exam. Forget about that school rehearsal. I know. So I, so he went and told his teacher what I said. And his teacher said, well, I'm going to say, well he's right. Well the leader of the band ordered him, but the leader of the band, the professor, he knowed that he was right too. See back in them days, you'd be glad to miss the exam, you'd laugh at the other guys that got to go to the bathroom. You're going to pass anyhow, they're going to mock you up, but still the kids would make it, would take that exam. See, when things come up, they'd ask, is this a widespread, would you scratch your head, you had a wait for somebody else to answer if it's a widespread. You wouldn't call it in the way, it's white or green, you know what I mean? It happened. What
do you want to say? When you're playing with those trios, what

kind of music did you play with those string groups? Well it's the same music we play in the day when they call it Dixonite. There's no such thing as Dixonite. It's ragtime music. Ragtime music. You see, it was a different title in that music back in those days. And you take your rumbles, you see. People tell you they want ragtime music, or they want hunky-tonk music. Hunky-tonk music was slow blues. See? Now you take your rumbles, your rumbles is a saloon poker. See? Your tango, that was mizookas. So you find that back in your method. You ever look in the books and see it? Well that's the same thing, your rumbles and your tango's a day. Now your blues is hunky-tonk music. Don't hide that old band up there, nothing but hunky-tonk music. That was some slow blues you could have been drawing on the floor. That's slow blues. Now the boogie woogie, that was hunky-tonk music. See? There was no boogie woogie. It was very slow. All night that same thing going like that. See? Is that so? Yeah. Very slow. Boogie was always in slow tempo? Huh? Boogie was always in slow tempo. Slow. It's blues. Blues is very slow. Now what was a slow drag? Well slow drag is the same. That's slow. They dance has a slow drag. See? It's a dance, it's called a slow drag. Did they play the blues when they danced? They played a very slow blues. You'd just be skating on the floor and grinding on the floor.
Was it like a 12 bar blues?

Yeah. Well it's not a, you couldn't say it's a 12 bar blues because they'll all make 20 bars and they'll say this. I see. And it's just very slow, you walk into that same temple all night long. And the places they call tunks. Now a tunk, you'll know you won't know what a tunk is. A tunk is where sometimes you have a piano playing in there and they're serving whiskey and everything else in this place. Say you get a glass of whiskey, a glass of beer was like this for a nickel. You can get from a nickel drink, the highest drink they had in those tunk was 15 cents. That's your best whiskey, 15 cents. Whiskey. For a glass of it? Yeah, for a little. For a glass. A glass is bigger than with redoxin and you had a glass of whiskey. Just like a glass of beer was like this for a nickel. So you pay it. For a pint of whiskey it wasn't more than 50 cents. See, you didn't have nothing but points. But you could go to a barrel house and buy a nickel worth of second best whiskey, the barrel whiskey. The barrel house, I don't know if you've ever seen what you call a barrel house, it's a big bar and it's got barrels sitting on racks all around, you know, around the wall, see. Oh yeah? Yeah, all around the wall. You go in there and get second best whiskey. Well you go to either one of those boughs and get you a second best whiskey. They had another drink they used to call Angelica. That's what it's called. What was it called? Angelica. See, now you get a cup like this for a nickel, see. Not for a dime, a big cup like that. Now you drink one of those cups, you got enough to lash it. What was that? Angelica. It's, it tastes like sherry wine but it wasn't sherry wine, and that's the sherry wine, see. That's what it's called, the sheep girl's sherry wine. Now your best sherry wine was that was twenty-five cents a quart back in the day. What did those tonks look like? Well tonks, they're just a, they're just a old saloon like in the front, they got a big room in the back with a piano in it, no chairs. On his chair in there they go with the piano sitting on. See. And they get in there and dance and they leave them dancing and go to the bar like this, the trunk here, the back here, well this would be the front that's the bar in there. The bar, there wouldn't be no big bar, it'd be about lungs as big, there's nothing to, see. Well the baby roger that guy had to get the best piano player, the guy who played the best blues, he had to make his crowd back in the day, see. That's what the trunk looked like. There's some big, what do you call it, funky room. Not clean, but dirty. They go in there with all the walls on and everything. Go anyway. When people went there did they take their own girls with them or did they have girls in those places? No, no, no. See back in those days, cabarets, you never take no girls to cabarets. They always had the girls. You ever went to one of those jitney dances where the girls stand in the middle of the floor wait for you to come and ask them to buy tickets?
Yes.

Well back in those days that's just where the cabarets used to run, but still in buying the tickets from the girls, you'll buy them a drink. See that's the cabaret I was playing. You buy them a drink, well a bottle of beer was 25 cents. Well the house made 15 cents. See they tied that ticket in half. She gets a dime.
Yes.

See she gets a dime. She don't get paid away this cabaret. She gets a dime. I think she gets something like 25 or 50 cents a night. Good cabaret, they keep the good girls there. They pay them, you know, like 50 cents a night.
Where was this cabaret that you worked at?
Across the Malls and Liberty. Yeah.
Oh no. How do girls dress?

What do they wear? They wear like nice gay them dresses, clean. It's regular dresses. Yeah. See women's land made their money on their legs, big legs. And you see the legs up to the air back in those days, man. Rain, I used to pay a dime to go downtown, a nickel. I used to see women get on the street called Ray's dress up so I could look at the legs. Because you didn't see no look at the wood of dresses starting. Oh I see, yeah. That thing going? Yeah. Yeah. That's good. And now the cribs, you see that was in the red light district. See, now the girl, now if you want to go out with the girl, see, 50 cents a dollar, whatever you want to give her, you know. And when she finishes with you, she come on back, get ready to go to the dance and give her. Oh you mean the girls have their cribs, but they will come to the dance? They'll come to the dance, but they'll all have a place where they go. See, they all had a place to go. They're sporting girls, you know. Yes, I understand. Sometimes it'd be right upstairs. The boss would have a place where they go, take you upstairs in the room, you see. Or you pay for the room. What was the name of this cabaret where you were? Hans Nagel. What? Hans Nagel and Eddie Groce, that's what they named it. Oh, I see. See, Hans Nagel, he was a Jew, but I don't know what Eddie Groce, I don't know what he was, but he was very quiet. He was a nice man.
What kind of a band did they have there? We had a seven-piece band.
A seven-piece band. King all over. Uh-huh. That was in 19… In 19… In 19… In 19… In 19… In 19… In 19… In 19… In 19…
Where were you? It's a good question. I'd like to know.

But there were some good days then. See, now that cabaret, now that job paid $9 a week. We made $15 and $20 a night tips. And we had a guy who used to pass the hat around the street, you know, to largely pass the hats at all the tables. And we had girls in there, very good girls, worked with the band, you know. We knew when it was a good party, she'd make the guys give me money. Yeah. We made more money off the German ships running in New Orleans, you know, the German ships running in New Orleans. And they didn't know they'd be in a good time. You ever been to have anybody, you can tell them the Germans would be in a good time. Because I was over there in 52 and I lived in the Red Light District over there. I said, this is once I got a chance to go back and see it. You know what I mean? Yeah, sure. And if you ever go over there, have a chance to go to Hamburg, before you finish this book, you go to a place they call St. Paulie in Hamburg. Yeah. St. Paulie. I've heard about it. And just the way they do down there, just the way they did in the old days, you just can picture it.
Is that so?
Yeah. Only thing they don't have the slow blues, see they're playing any kind of music, but it's still a Red Light District.
Yeah.

Women's calling you, you're passing close to the window, they're calling you. If you're wearing a hat, they'll take your hat, so you're going to come in and get your hat and all that stuff. Yeah, it was some good days. And I've seen them go, and I went over there and seen it. I had a nice hotel, man, downtown. Yeah. Just paid for it. I couldn't stay. I would rent me another hotel room. I would rent you a little bit.
It's a random day of the good old days, huh? Yeah.

The bus had to pass and pick me up when we were going with the bus driver nowhere I was. And they said, I know Al Foster, we passed and pick him up. It rolled a horn, the guns, and it pops. Are you ready? They would come playing a bunch of the guns and bring me up to the bus.
I wish you'd tell us a little more about, before you came to New Orleans, out in the country, you know, what kind of places did you play at?

Well, you see I was born on this farm, see, and my daddy, well I hardly played, if I went to the house, I was a little bit of a dance, and I would call it a ball, they'd want to know that you'd get 15 or 20 people in the dance that night, you had a lot of people, see. Because my daddy used to get this on this farm. Who came people from? Different parts of the other plantations came to this. Where did you have the dance? Where did you get it? In the empty house we could find, they could find back those days, see. And then all the plantations got the high dancers done after me and my brother, that's big enough to play. We used to play, sometimes my uncle would be playing, like one plantation we'd be playing on another one, we played better music than my uncle, we'd draw the crowd. My uncle used to get mad with my daddy. Going to ruin those kids, should be able to sleep and he used to fuss it. I used to get salty with my daddy. Well, I didn't want to play no music, I was a hard guy. I was mean. He's dead, sir. Very mean when I was small. I did everything to keep on playing music. But your father wanted you to be a musician, huh? Yeah, but he'd have to treat me, sir, because I was the only one where I was scared of him, but my brother was there, Fred, and I wasn't a senior. I would go, I'd have to go, but how would I play? Like sometimes when he wanted some whiskey or some cigars he'd take us somewhere to serenade, like you would go to serenade your father, we'd get a lot of whiskey and we'd get some cakes and candies.
How old were you when you first started to play in places like?
Well I was playing cello then, see. Around six or seven.
Did you ever play on homemade instruments? Yeah.
My brother made me a barrel bass before I got the cello.
When was it made up?

You ever seen a little flower barrels, the old time flower barrels with the barrel states, the flower, which used to send years ago? It's a barrel. Like a regular barrel? Yeah, but it's very thin, like a regular barrel, see. Used to sell flowers all over the country, ain't it? Oh. That's what it used to be. Well he used to get the big ones and he used to get the half a barrel, you know. Well he'd take that and cut it out and put some strings on it.
What kind of strings were they?
Some twine. Twine. What did he have? Did it have a neck to it? Yeah, he made a neck and fixed it so he could tune it.
How many strings did you have? Three. Three strings.
All the bass players, Eddie Corbidora band, but I was playing three string bass. I'm one of the rips. Is he older than you at Garland? Yeah. He's older than you. Yeah. He's up in the 70s.
He gave a seven one order, he's way up in the 70s, two. I didn't want to say 70.
And then, in 1905 I was in school and the order was on that plane, I was living up in the 70s. Uh huh. And George. He's older than me too. I know that.
That's my father.
There's a nice people that father named him. Yeah.
Yeah, I know the world. So when did you start to play on regular instruments? Did you have little kid bands when you had those? No.

You see we had a kid in a town called Donaldsonville. He played violin. Well we tried to get him in the band with us, my brother played guitar, but we never could get nowhere with him so well. By the time I made my brother go, we'd have to hire a man to play guitar with us, some other guy to play guitar with us. And the kids would try to play but it wasn't there, you know what I mean? Yeah.
But who taught you how to play?
See my brother, my uncle, my father's brother, taught my brother. And my brother taught me my sister.
Did you ever play other instruments besides bass?

Bass and I tried to play a little guitar. Most of them, most of the bass. See when I, now I started playing, I started playing the first string bass that my brother bought, I think around 97, big bass, he bought me. You mean a regular instrument? Bass, yeah. Can I interrupt you for a minute?
Yeah. What are you going to be in the hotel all afternoon? All afternoon. All afternoon, I'll be back up then I'll see you.
Leave me something for you, Lord, that's part of the other side because he's too heavy.
Now look, Pops.
Can you get out that door, man? You can barely make it, George.
You can barely make it. I'll tell her how old you really are. We'll be here, George.
Now you see. See, I was playing along before I figured out in 97. How many years would that be?
Nineteen seven is fifty years ago. Exactly. Nineteen fifty-seven. That made me buck. Nineteen seven you'd be fifteen years old. Yeah, I was playing a long before that.
Well, that's when I grew up in the big band. See, because I was playing good eight years before that.
Really?

As far as I can remember back, because I know I was around seven, six or seven. You see, that's the closest I'll get back to when I started, because I don't know when I started. See, I figured my husband had been around six or seven. Which would be about 1900, 1902, something like that.
Yeah, about 1900. Wait a minute. In 1900 you were eight years old.
Wait a minute, wait a minute. 1902, my mother carried me to New Orleans.
You were ten years old then?
Yeah, around ten or eleven, between ten and eleven. The seat of Mardi Gras.
Is that the first time you went to the city?
Yeah, because I made 11 years old that year I think. See. And well I was playing before that.
You weren't playing before that?

See, because my brother, see the McCall, the people that we raised, he got married I think in 1900. I remember driving him to the station. My brother? No. The McCalls, the people that we raised, the sons. See I had to go with them to drive the buggy back, because they got to trade and they go to New Orleans. And I went after they got settled, about 1901. They were in Mardi Gras. See my brother was in New Orleans, he was in New Orleans about a year from when my mother met there. They got married in 1901, in the summer time, and we went to New Orleans, the next year, February. But we was playing before then, around there, because they broke up our little band. So when you went to? When my brother went to New Orleans, to work for those people. He was waiting tables like my daddy was doing, see. Then my mother moved there. Then my mother went to New Orleans, and we was in New Orleans about a place or not to be speaking. So dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
Pops Foster, April 21st, 1957, Rule 2.

It was around 1997 and 1999 when my brother bought that big bass for me. Uh-huh. He had left working for McCall's and he started working with a little band, a guy called Roy Palmer. Roy Palmer, yes. Roy Palmer was our guitar player. You had to see what became a trombone player? No, let me see what Roy was playing. Roy was playing trumpet. Uh-huh. And Joe Johnson was our guitar player. So Joe Johnson learned trumpet and Roy Palmer and Roy Palmer was good too. Joe died. That's what I tell the guys, they read about who they don't know. See? They read about the guys they know, see? But they had great trumpet players. I mean he was a hell of a white trumpet player, Joe Johnson. He was very good. His name was Joe Johnson? Joe Johnson, yeah. He was about the trumpet player and Freddie Kepler was a little loud trumpet player. He was a little loud trumpet player. He was a little loud trumpet player. Did you hear Baldwin? Yeah, when I was a kid. See, because Freddie, we made up a band. Eddie Goyle sent me on the job was with Freddie Kepler's brother. Louie? Louie Kepler. And I didn't know Louie was there. Louie and them had a band downtown. When I went on the job to play with Louie and them, they were trying to get a kid band. Well, that was just the thing they wanted, see? That was the biggest. Then all the bands downtown, the Imperial Band and the bands with Freddie always wanted to fight every time somebody wanted to take me out of the way up with his brother's band. Freddie wanted to fight. Freddie wanted to fight, you know? It was all right for me to play with his band, because I used to play in John Lindsay's plays sometimes, Freddie's band. Well, John Lindsay and I looked so much alike people didn't know what it is that Johnny Reed was me playing sometimes, see? Freddie wanted to fight all the time. I tell you, every time Marilyn was hiring me to play with him, and he'd get in a fight. And then King Oliver won't fight about me once. Then me and Freddie wanted to fight. Well, it wasn't no knife, it was fist, you know? So I can explain to you exactly, the closer I'd get around 19, between 7 and 9 when I first started playing string bass. But when I started, I had to be, I had to be in that, around 6. I know I was old, because I didn't start to walk and I sat on, man. I had terrified my litter. And I stopped walking, I didn't walk until I was around 5. Oh yeah. Is that so? And it had to be around 6 or 7 when I started playing. And I didn't want to play. I didn't want to do it with riding horses. That's all I used to like to do. Do you remember that first Mardi Gras that you saw? 1902, not so well. 1902. Were there a lot of brass bands? Oh yeah. They always did a lot of brass bands. I remember them when my mother came in. That's not their first one. Well that was about their first and the older one. Because after that, every year, I was, it was many years after that, every year, I was in the parade myself.
Sure. Why would you play? Bass drum?

I would be playing on one of those wagons, see? You'd be at the wagons. Oh I see. Like a bunch of you guys, like you say, you got about eight guys that are ready to get a big furniture wagon. Put your little band, get your three or six piece band in, wagon, build a wagon. The guy would be hanging all around the wagon, riding all over the town, see?
